speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I would ask unanimous consent to make the following motion concerning the Competition Act which involves substantial changes in Canadian law and the regulation of trade and commerce and deals in several sections with matters of provincial jurisdiction. It is imperative that the question of constitutionality be tested before the bill is passed and implemented. I would therefore ask unanimous consent to move as follows:
That the Competition Act, and in particular Parts 3, 4, 5 and 6, be referred forthwith to the Supreme Court of Canada in order that the Court may give an opinion as to whether any parts of the said act are ultra vires.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent importance. On the basis of the unemployment figures released today, reflecting the persistent lack of confidence of the business community in the economy, and judging by the fact that part-time jobs created exceeded the total jobs created by 14,000, and because of the fact that unemployment with its multifold social and economic implications continues to increase, I would therefore like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski):
That this House request the government to make a full and definitive statement to the country on its economic goals and expectations for the remainder of the fiscal year, and declare, as well, its contingency plans to alleviate hardship on all people and families who will not find jobs this winter.

speechtext:
1.	Is the Bank of Canada giving consideration to the collection of data on the volume of bank loans outstanding and total money supply by region?
2.	Is Statistics Canada giving consideration to the development of a system of regional accounts?
3.	What statistical series are now prepared on a regional basis?
4.	Is there a study group or task force in Statistics Canada concerned with the development of comprehensive regional statistics?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Jerome (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am informed by the Bank of Canada and Statistics Canada as follows:
1.	The regional domicile of the bank loans and bank deposits of nation-wide enterprises which deal with nation-wide banks is not meaningful; loans arranged in one region are frequently drawn on for use in other regions, and similarly deposit balances carried in one region may arise from operations in, or be destined for disbursement in, other regions. Consequently, collecting or estimating figures for total money supply and bank loans on a regional basis would not provide information useful for the analysis of regional economic problems. However, the Bank of Canada is examining whether there may be some sub-categories of chartered bank assets which might be collected to provide meaningful regional data.
2.	No. However, Statistics Canada is working towards an enlarged regional economic data base which, when developed further, would be useful in constructing regional accounts.
3.	Statistics Canada is preparing an increasing number of statistical series on a regional basis. A large number of series are now published in the demographic field, the labour field, in industrial areas and others on regional basis and further efforts are being made in this direction.
4.	Yes.

LOAN GRANTED BY CANADA TO MALAYSIA
speechtext:
1.	What was the amount of the loan granted by Canada to Malaysia when the Prime Minister of that country visited Canada?
2.	What is the duration of the loan?
3.	What is the rate of interest of the loan?
4.	What are the reimbursement terms?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LOAN GRANTED BY CANADA TO MALAYSIA
speechtext:
1. Canada has agreed to make available to the Government of Malaysia a Loan in an amount which is not to exceed $46,500,000.
2.	The duration of the loan will commence from the first withdrawal of principal and terminate on the date to which final repayment is complete. Final repayment of principal is to take place on or before March 31, 2001.
3.	The rate of interest of the loan is to be calculated at 3 per cent per annum on the principal amount of the loan drawn by Malaysia and outstanding.
4.	Reimbursement will be made in 46 equal semi-annual instalments of the principal amount of the loan which is utilized by Malaysia, due and payable on the last day of September and March in each year commencing on September 30, 1978 and ending March 31, 2001. Payment of interest will similarly be made in semi-annual instalments due and payable on September 30 and March 31 in each year commencing from the first withdrawal of principal. Payment of interest will be calculated on the outstanding balance of the principal. The principal of and the interest charges on the loan are to be paid without any deduction whatsoever and in particular will be free from any taxes, charges, or other restrictions imposed under the Laws of Malaysia. The loan will be utilized on the basis of contracts won by Canadian suppliers in international competition. Consequently, the exact amount of the loan which will be utilized cannot presently be determined.

NATIONAL DEFENCE MANPOWER STRENGTHS-MEMBER SERVING IN VARIOUS WARS
speechtext:
1.	How many Canadians served in (a) the Boer War (b) the First World War (c) the Second World War (d) the Korean War?
2.	How many Canadians served in more than one of the above-mentioned wars?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE MANPOWER STRENGTHS-MEMBER SERVING IN VARIOUS WARS
speechtext:
1. It is not possible to give an accurate reply to this question as it is impossible to state precisely

how many Canadians served in each of these wars because Canadian citizenship was not established until after the Second World War. Many Americans and others served in the Canadian Forces, some concealing their nationality to do so, and many others resident in Canada travelled to the United Kingdom to join the British Forces. However, as far as can be determined, the numbers were as follows: (a) 7,368 including those who served in the South African Constabulary; (b) 626,636; in addition, a large number, probably between 15,000 and 20,000 was recruited in Canada for the British Air Services; (c) 1,086,343; (d) 25,583.
2. The number of Canadians who served in more than one of these wars can only be ascertained by reviewing the records of all who enlisted in the services between 1897 and 1954. The necessary staff to undertake the large amount of work that this would entail is not available.

Mr. Chairman, there was considerable debate last Friday and again yesterday on the implications of income splitting and I think it might be useful to the committee to appreciate the significance of it in terms of dollars and cents. In the first place one must note that the options that have been advanced by members opposite would not be available to wage earners; they would only be available to the self-employed.
Second, there has been some talk about people being able to resolve this situation for themselves by incorporating. I suppose that is quite true, but the people who do incorporate take the disadvantages of incorporation as well as the advantages. It is not all clear sailing. In the 1969 tax year, for which we have the most recent 1971 edition of taxation statistics, the average self-employed physician or surgeon in Canada reported a gross income of $32,338. The average self-employed business proprietor reported an average income of $6,485. For the convenience of some calculations, and in order to give the benefit of the doubt all around, I have rounded the doctor's figure down to $32,000 from $32,338, and the self-employed business proprietor's figure up to $6,500. The significance here is the difference that this advantage would give to the higher income people.
Basically, assuming no dependent children and assuming that the doctor employed his wife as a nurse in the business and paid her $10,000 of his $32,000 income, the tax instead of being $11,549.85, which it would be on his income of $32,000, would be reduced to $9,636.25, or a saving for that family of $1,913.60. On the other hand, for the self-employed business proprietor-
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Is the hon. member for Athabasca rising on a point of order?

Yes, Mr. Chairman. I raise the point of order that the parliamentary secretary is attempting to deceive the House by giving an income tax figure for a gross income. I think this is ridiculous. You have to use net income.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I could, of course, have run through the figures for exemptions and standard deductions and brought it down to taxable income, and so on, but I thought since those are matters of record these figures might have served. I have calculated the tax against this income, assuming there were no children and taking the standard $100 deduction in lieu of charitable donations, for medical expenses, and so on. So for the professional man, the doctor who was near the average income for doctors in 1969, and applying table 2 in the "Summary of 1971 Tax Reform Legislation" we have a saving, as a result of that splitting of $32,000 into $22,000 for the doctor and $10,000 for his wife, of $1,913.60.
For the business proprietor whose business income that year was $6,485-and I have assumed here $6,500-we have a tax, after application of the same criteria, of $884.65. If he splits his income in much the same way by employing his wife in the front end of his store, keeps $4,500 taxable income himself and pays her $2,000, he reduces his and his wife's tax to a total of $783.64, a saving of $101.01. So I think the committee will see very obviously, Mr. Chairman, that the advantages hon. members are advocating would certainly accrue not to the small business proprietor but to the high income, professional person.
This is a lot of nonsense, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary talks about a doctors' gross income being $32,000. Does he take into account the rooms that are required, often in high-cost areas, all the equipment that is necessary in the carrying on of a medical practice? I think this is a very unfair way to present the matter. There is another question I want to ask him. Supposing a doctor and his wife are practising in the same building, he is an obstetrician and she is a pediatrician-what becomes of that income? How does the minister rate them?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the income figure, when I used the term gross income, of course is his business income after he has received his fees and deducted all the costs of doing business. This is the figure that is plugged into the income tax return, from which deductions and exemptions are taken off in calculating taxable income.

You did not answer the second part of my question. If a husband and wife are both practising, one is an obstetrician and one is a pediatrician, how do you rate their incomee? How do you apply this principle to them?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If it is a partnership-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Then there is no problem. If it is a partnership there would be a problem, but if they are just sharing offices and carrying oh independent practices there is no problem.
In other words, you treat those two differently than you would if they were working in a store?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think during the debate on the proposals in the white paper there was an effort to try to identify business corporations with their shareholders, and so on. That concept was rather emphatically rejected by the business community which made representations to us. There is indeed a difference in the way you conduct your business. There is a tax difference that flows from the way the business is conducted.

There is very definite discrimination here. A man's wife could have been running a business of her own up the street, or could have been running it in the same store and they could both come together. This is plain discrimination, and the parliamentary secretary knows it.

I am very pleased that the parliamentary secretary has sought to enlighten us on this point. I raised it in at least two of my presentations to the committee. This question of net income after taxes is very relevant to low income people. I am not so worried about people with a gross income of $25,000 or $30,000, but I am worried about those with a $6,500 family income. It is all very well to pass the tax off as only $100 or $200, but with inflation and the high cost of living today that extra $100 or $200 in tax is a very serious matter to the low income group.
I am not particularly worried about what happens to the combined income of two well paid professionals. As a matter of fact, I think that the sliding scale of income tax has a great deal to do with this group which is already carrying a large burden of taxation. When one takes into account the years spent at college and the overhead which a doctor, let us say, has to face for clinics, equipment, X-ray material, and so on, the net return for a lifetime of hard work is not as exaggerated as it appears to many people. My emphasis is not on that type of situation. I am concerned with the family that has a gross income of $6,500-the mamma and papa store and many small businesses which require the work and co-operation of the whole family including the children.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, I wonder if the hon. member appreciates that in those circumstances the children can be hired and paid. The only effect that has is to reduce the exemptions they are entitled to when claiming the children, because the children have income.

Yes, I understand that there are ways if you seek hard enough. Another difficulty is the bookkeeping that is necessary. I am not against the benefits that we have in Canada, but the bookkeeping that the small income family has to do is hardly worth while. Perhaps we can make it unnecessary to take this $100 away from small income families when there is an inequity in the legislation as the parliamentary secretary admits. It is not

merely a case of saying that some higher income groups have to pay the taxes; we know they have to pay on a much higher scale. I am worried about the net income payable to a family trying to keep a small business open when there is very little escape under this tax bill.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment on what the parliamentary secretary said about income when the husband and wife are partners. I think he should clear up this question. In his example he cited incomes of $6,500 and $32,000. I think he really meant net income before taxes, because for the professional worker gross income usually means all profit before any deductions for office expenses. Probably this is why there was some misunderstanding.
I think the parliamentary secretary should point out the problem of the professional man who spends many years in studying. Sometimes he is 35 years of age before he makes any income. During this period of his professional life he spends a great deal of his own money and savings on furthering his education. At age 50 he is no further ahead than many people who went into the labour force much earlier in life. This is something we must look at in the future. Income averaging may have a little value, but not very much at this time.
Where a husband and wife are partners in business I think this is discrimination against other people in business. I think it is safe to say that the whole thrust of taxation is against people who wish to be in business. Usually they operate on a cash basis and the wife is often involved, working in the corner store. Canada needs this type of business because of our small and scattered population, particularly in rural areas.
I think the government is making a mistake by not recognizing that there are many valid reasons for treating husband and wife as partners in the business, and I think most farms could be classified as a husband and wife partnership to some extent. This section does not seem to be different from the old act and does nothing to help the small business. With the further capitalization necessary in the small business, the progressive income tax takes more and more income and leaving less for capital savings. There is no help for these people in this section of the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is no exemption on government of Canada bonds and the interest on them. There is, in some instances, an exemption with respect to withholding tax in cases where foreign owners have bought a general issue of government of Canada bonds which buyers are not taxable in the countries in which they reside. The general situation is that bond interest from government of Canada bonds is taxable in the hands of the recipient. Tax may be postponed by not clipping the coupons and by holding them to maturity. Quite often people aged, say, 55 buy Canada Savings Bonds and hold on to them for ten years. They may cash them when their income is lower and include all the amount received as income.
They have the option, even though they do not clip their coupons, to take the amount that would be received into account with respect to income if they so desire. However, once you move to an accrual basis, you must do that with respect to all interest earned. The same rules apply to non-government bonds. That is, unless the coupons are cashed they do not constitute part of income.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

This particular plan is one which is funded by an employer who deducts his contributions from his taxable income. [Mr. Gilbert.J

Income Tax Act
open to the individual taxpayer. I see no reason why there should not be a provision whereby an individual taxpayer, because of the nature of his business, the nature of his income earning, should not be able to at least have an opportunity to establish his taxation year other than on a strictly calendar year basis.
I recognize that there does have to be some control over this matter, otherwise it would produce a good deal of confusion and difficulty for the department. I would certainly not object to some control being built in either in terms of variance from the calendar year procedure or leaving it to the discretion or concurrence of the minister. This is certainly in line with many other provisions of the act. But it seems to me that in some cases there is a good case for establishing other than a calendar year. I hope the government would find it possible to qualify this section in such a way that the individual taxpayer in Canada can qualify for variance from the calendar year provision in the same way as a corporation. I hope to have a response from the government on this matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member is quite correct. A corporation is free to establish its fiscal year in the initial year in which it starts business. It requires the consent of the Minister of National Revenue to change that year thereafter. So I do not think there is any significant element of tax deferral, and certainly no element of tax avoidance is implicit in the date selected for the fiscal year. What may be postponed in the initial instance is caught up once the company starts operating on a regular basis. There is no real advantage.
However, the hon. member may be under some misapprehension when he refers to the individual taxpayer engaged in a business. Business proprietors are also entitled to select their own year and determine their income during the year for the business. Then the proprietor himself, of course, includes his income, or the partner includes his share of the partnership income in his personal income for that year and pays tax on it the following April 30.
I do not know how many sections of this bill would have to be amended if we were to give individual taxpayers the option to pick their year. The dates on which quarterly instalments are made by people with significant amounts of investment and professional income would have to be made flexible to meet that situation. The dates upon which penalties apply, and many other dates, would be up for revision and would have to be made flexible. I am not really satisfied that it is a workable solution.
The trauma of having the national tax paying day on April 30 every year is one that the taxpayer seems to have become accustomed to on a regular basis. Perhaps it is the sort of thing that one would just as soon get over once and for all, rather than having various people on the block reporting their income tax on a weekly basis and the matter becoming a topic of general conversation 52 weeks a year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Regina East pursuing this matter?

I just wish to deal with the comments of the parliamentary secretary. I recognize, of course, that in the provisions which are set out for a corporation it does not

November 10, 1971
Income Tax Act
involve tax avoidance or tax deferral in any way to use a period other than the calendar year. Certainly it was not my intention to suggest any such thing. Nevertheless, it is a matter of convenience for many corporations to establish for their own reasons a fiscal period which is other than the calendar year, and as a further convenience for taxation purposes this fiscal period is deemed to be, in effect, the taxation year. But when it comes to an individual, the parliamentary secretary pointed out that some businesses and proprietors of businesses as such are able to use a period other than the calendar year.
I am not clear whether it is possible for farmers, fishermen and other occupational groups engaged in economic activity which is other than a wage earning type of activity, to take advantage of this provision and I would appreciate having this point clarified. The parliamentary secretary also seems to throw up some road blocks in terms of the mechanical difficulties that would be involved in making a change to this section. I am not too impressed with that point. It seems to me it might be possible to work in an amendment along the lines of stipulating that the tax year in the case of an individual is the calendar year or, if the minister gives his consent, a period other than the calendar year shall be deemed to be the taxation year.
I do not pretend to be an expert in drafting law, but it should be a relatively simple matter to make an appropriate amendment if there were the desire or will to do so. I hope we will have some response from the parliamentary secretary beyond what he has already indicated.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: First, Mr. Chairman, I am not aware of any provision that would prevent farmers or fishermen choosing any year other than the calendar year, although I am sure, from practice and custom, that very few of them do so. Before the hon. member seriously suggests that an individual on wage or salary be allowed to select his own tax year, he might like to discuss the matter with the treasurer or controller of the federated co-ops to see how they would handle the issue of T-4 slips, accounting for Canada Pension Plan contributions, their own registered retirement saving plans contributions and the other tax deductions they have made within a 365-day period for their several thousand employees, all of whom no doubt would have exercised the option. So that at least a few of those details would have to be issued daily, rather than as a chore which is faced up to once a year for each employee. I think that the hon. member, on reflection, would agree that this would be a rather horrendous administrative burden to foist upon Canadian employers.

Mr. Chairman, I have had experience in doing accounting work for co-operative organizations, and for the information of the parliamentary secretary I do have fairly good knowledge on the matter. In this age of computers and mechanical systems available to undertake such work, I am sure that where there is a will there is a way to solve whatever administrative problems would arise. In fact, I am not sure that this matter has been of great concern in the minds of those drafting some of the other provisions of the bill.
(Mr. Burton.]

Mr. Chairman, in regard to this section on the taxation year and the difference in the treatment of corporations and individuals there is a point to be made, because in many businesses there are specific trading patterns, or buying and selling patterns, and the individual in business may not find it convenient to have the calendar year as his taxation year.
I can think of an example that is very common in my own business of farming and ranching. Often, as a result of pressures exerted in the industry due to feed shortages or market fluctuations of one kind or another, there are forced sales where in fact two complete cash crops have to be sold in one year. In this situation we have the individual, rather than paying the much higher tax that he would have to pay if his income were distributed over two years being forced into the marketplace around the end of the year, about Christmas time, and having to make a purchase of livestock. And he may not even take the livestock he purchases back to his place of business; he may leave them in a public stockyard until New Year's Day so that he can qualify for a fairer level of taxation on his business. In such circumstances I cannot see why we cannot treat an individual on the same basis as a corporation.
Maybe we could use the criterion of having 80 per cent or 90 per cent of the shares of a corporation owned by the family or the individual in question. This is a subject we discussed the other day when sections 28 to 32 were before the committee. A brief from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture indicated they thought it would be fair if the family corporation in which 80 per cent or 90 per cent of the shares were owned by the individual in question could be treated the same as an individual taxpayer, taking into account the $1,000 exemption on homes and similar provisions. I think it is only fair that the minister should consider extending this option to the individual so far as the definition of "taxation year" is concerned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member misunderstood or did not hear the answer that I gave the hon. member for Regina East. Certainly there is no reason why a farmer, fisherman or small business proprietor cannot choose his fiscal year. It is his personal income tax that is due on April 30 each year for the previous calendar year, but for business purposes, if it suits his convenience and if there is some advantage to him, he is entitled-the same as a corporation-to pick any one of the 365 days in a year that suits his purposes and, I suppose, his auditor's convenience.

Mr. Chairman, I realize the date can be switched once, but I believe there is some difficulty with the department in shifting the date for the year's end more than once. This is something which would have to be looked at very carefully because of the incidence of tax avoidance. But there should be some leeway provided.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
A businessman is in exactly the same position as a corporation. He may, with the approval of the Minister of National Revenue, change the date of his fiscal year end. The criterion is that it must be for a bona fide business reason. If he were anticipating a very significant amount of income in a particular period, he might have difficulty convincing the minister that his intention
November 10, 1971

in changing his year end is not to defer tax but is for a legitimate business reason. For example, if you propose to merge two companies you can go to the minister and get this permission in order to have all financial statements dovetailed, and start with a clean sheet. There are many legitimate reasons for changing the year end. I suppose "frequently" would not be the correct word, but these changes are not an unusual occurrence.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to be irreverent for about ten seconds and then report an injustice. One distinguished taxpayer was born on February 29 and he annually reports a very substantial income. If the parliamentary secretary's words were to be taken literally, I wonder how much income tax Henri Richard of the Montreal Canadians would pay. He might decide to make his peace with the Income Tax Department every four years instead of every year.
The injustice probably fits in with the general idea of what the taxation year is, and arises out of the circumstances of some Canadians whose income is derived entirely from investment. These investments may be timed through the year so that the first interest payment comes in June and the second in October. As I understand the existing regulations, they can be asked to make four payments a year on those investments. The first payment would take place in March before they had received any income whatever from the investments for that year. I do not want to belabour the point and I only raise it because I think it is an injustice which can be cured by making the regulations more flexible.
These people could be given an option on when the payments start. I do not expect an answer this afternoon but I would expect the parliamentary secretary to say that this question would be looked into.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, we certainly will look into it.

I have a question related to the question of the hon. member for Battle River. Am I to understand, assuming that an incorporated businessman has multiple income, that he can select a date, say October 31, for a particular business but still report the following April his personal income tax?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is correct. He can select that his business or medical practice operate on a fiscal year basis starting November 1 and ending October 31. The income up to October 31 would be income for that year and he would pay tax the following April 30. The income he earned in business during November and December would be carried forward and not be reported as personal income until the following year, and any tax paid in respect of it until April 30 the succeeding year.
Of course, instalment payments such as the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants mentioned would be paid throughout on that professional income because it is not subject to deduction at source.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder what the situation would be if we had a new tax bill reported to be coming in on January 1 and an individual or small corporation with
Income Tax Act
a year end of September 30. Bringing this forward in terms of capital cost allowance, in the depreciation schedule what will the effect be, or how will the taxpayer react to the year end at the end of September and the new system coming in at the beginning of January, in regard to these items.
Will he have to take this interim period and have another tax report filed for those three months? Will the same rules that held under the depreciation schedule hold true until the end of the calendar year so that any item he buys before the end of the calendar year will be recorded under the old tax act? Would the parliamentary secretary clarify this situation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
For corporations there will be proration and, for example, if their fiscal year runs from July 1 to the end of June they would have to calculate the tax on half their income on the basis of the present act and half on the basis of the new act.
For individuals there is no problem. They move into a calendar year and the individual tax system is applicable for that whole year. For the proprietor who derives his income from a business, if he derives it from a business until October 31 this year, that is all taxable under the present system. In effect, the income he has deferred for November and December this year would be picked up and he would not receive it as personal income until 1972, and it would be taxable under the new system. There is no proration of personal tax necessary under the new system.

I noted the parliamentary secretary said that farmers, fishermen and any unincorporated type of business enterprise can take advantage of the provision to have the taxation year on a basis other than the calendar year. I accept the parliamentary secretary's word that such is the case. I believe he indicated that he knew of nothing that would prevent a farmer or fisherman using a fiscal period other than the calendar year.
I have before me a copy of the 1970 Farmers and Fishermen's Tax Guide. I have looked through it quite carefully. I may have missed something, but I see absolutely nothing in it that points out to the taxpayer that he can choose a period other than the calendar year-this would be with respect to starting his operation-or that he can change that time period with the consent of the minister. There is nothing in the guide that points this out.
I am not doubting the parliamentary secretary's word, but if that is the case surely it would be reasonable to have a reference in the tax guide to that effect. It seems to me that this is quite inadequate. I agree that there may be many cases when it would not be used, but there are cases when it would. I think there should be provision in the law that consideration be given to problems facing individual taxpayers just as is the case with corporations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I shall certainly refer the hon. member's statement concerning the tax guide to the Minister of National Revenue. I do not have a copy in front of me so I cannot comment on it.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate what the parliamentary secretary has said and I hope there will be some follow-up because I feel this matter deserves further

November 10, 1971
Income Tax Act
attention. I therefore propose to move an amendment to section 249(l)(b) as follows:
Add after the word "year" in line 6 on page 580 the following: "except where the minister gives his consent to the individual
to use a fiscal period other than the calendar year".
I would commend this amendment to the committee because I think we should at least provide an opportunity for the individual taxpayer to have his case considered if he feels he has a case for using a period other than the calendar year. I might point out that the way I phrase this amendment sets the calendar year as the starting point and then simply opens the door to the possibility of a variation of the calendar year approach. I think it is very important that we should consider this question in terms of treating the individual taxpayer in the same way as we treat corporations.

On clause 1-Section 251: Arm's length.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would draw the attention of the committee to the amendment to this section, moved by the Minister of National Revenue on October 22, 1971, as recorded at page 8960 of Hansard for that date. Shall the amendment carry?
Amendment (Mr. Gray) agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, since there may be legitimate dealings within a family that may be at arm's length, and since these transactions may not be always recognized as being arm's length transactions, is there any recourse to appeal or other mechanism for people who wish to establish that the transaction they entered into would come under the purview of this section?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the section we are considering defines what is arm's length. To answer the hon. member's question I would need a concrete example of the type of transaction he is asking about. This section does not allow or prohibit anything; it simply defines what is arm's length. It is other sections of the bill, such as the ones that were dealt with at some length on Friday, which preclude non-arm's length transactions being entered into without incurring an element of tax. Tax would not be incurred if the people dealing with each other were totally unrelated.
That my wife and I are not at arm's length is not a rebuttable presumption. We are not. The bill precludes us from entering into certain business arrangements without my incurring a degree of taxation that I would not incur if I made the same deal with the hon. member opposite. So without knowing precisely what type of transaction he has in mind so that I may look at the substantive section of the bill and not the definition section in order to see whether the facts of the case fit into an arm's length relationship, I really cannot answer the question.

Mr. Chairman, I have a question to ask, the relevance of which will become apparent as time goes on. I know why these definitions have been incorporated into this particular section. I am curious about the procedures or remedies that will be open to people in cases where there is controversy as to whether a transaction is at arm's length or not. Perhaps I may give an exaggerated illustration to render my meaning clear. If a transaction takes place between me and my wife, it will not be considered as being at arm's length. But if there is a divorce and a subsequent remarriage and a transaction takes place between husband No. 1 and husband No. 2, what is the position? Is that, or is that not an arm's length transaction?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, that is at arm's length.

Mr. Chairman, I have a further question. That transaction is apparently at arm's length. Yet how will you determine, in cases of controversy, whether such a transaction preceded or did not precede the divorce?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the time of the transaction is a question of fact and those asserting that it took place at a certain time would have to establish that date. Also, any person suggesting that it took place at another time would have to sustain that position. That is the sort of thing that appeal boards and courts must determine fairly regularly.
Could I be more explicit. How will that determination be made? Will it be through a court action or through departmental regulation? How will the final decision be made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The initial determination would be made by the assessor. If the taxpayer does not agree with that determination he can appeal the assessment and take the matter right up to the Supreme Court of Canada if necessary.

Thank you. That answers my question.
November 10, 1971

Mr. Chairman, I have a short question. In some respects this country is still a great big parish and one is often startled to find how many cousins one can run into. Some cousins are kissing cousins and some are not. There are some cousins with whom, according to the laws of consanguinity, you can do certain things and there are cousins with whom, according to the laws of consanguinity, one cannot do certain things.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: They must be kept at arm's length.

Of course, there is no personal preference in this. Is there any definition of such relationships? It seems to me that you can legitimately do business with people who are distantly related to you by blood. Is there any definition as to where this blood relationship cuts off, so to speak, and where it does not? You will find such a definition in holy mother church and in other areas. Is there such a definition in the law?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, subsection (6) of section 251 defines the various areas of blood relationship where transactions are automatically deemed to be not at arm's length.
Would the parliamentary secretary repeat that subsection?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is subsection 6 on page 584 of the bill.

We again get into the question, particularly with new law, of estates and capital gains. Can we have an undertaking from the parliamentary secretary-I am sure we will-that should there be other changes when we deal with capital gains proper, we can have the option of reopening this section?

Yes, Mr. Chairman.

On clause 1-section 151: Estimate of tax

Mr. Chairman, under section 150, "Estimate of tax," I note there was an excess of tax collected in prepayments last year to the extent of 10 per cent of the total revenue of the government. It becomes a matter of who is a servant to whom, when we look at the estimate of tax and the way it is collected. When it reaches the point
Income Tax Act
where 10 per cent of the total funds are being returned to the taxpayer, it seems this is overdoing it. I realize that people die during the year, change employment or lose their jobs and become unemployed. A certain amount of tax collection over and above the amount that is necessary then becomes a fact of life.
We should carefully consider who is working for the convenience of whom. Does the taxpayer exist for the convenience of those who are supposed to work for him, or is the taxpayer a servant of the bureaucracy that exists in the department? I would like to hear this concept discussed, because it can get out of hand. Everything must be relevant.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member's concept is not accurate.

The parliamentary secretary says that my concept is not accurate. Are the figures that I quoted with regard to overcollection of taxes or refunds to the extent of approximately 10 per cent in the last year very far out? Which of my comments is not accurate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not aware of the figures the hon. member is quoting. Perhaps he should cite the source. I will be glad to check them against the source. However, his concept that the taxpayer exists as a servant of the bureaucracy is not, I suggest, accurate.

I do not have available the figures I was referring to but I can provide the parliamentary secretary with them at the beginning of next week. It was reported publicly that this was the case-that there was a 10 per cent overcollection of taxes and that this amount had been refunded. If this is the case-and I can provide the parliamentary secretary with the document which cited these figures-has the hon. gentleman any comment to make on this situation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think the hon. member will agree that in all fairness I should have an opportunity to see the figures before commenting on their significance.

I will provide the parliamentary secretary with the figures next week.
Clause 1, section 151, agreed to.

Agreed.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask some basic questions which have occurred to most taxpayers. They arise under this section. It is always a matter of concern to taxpayers that when an assessment is made with respect to any delinquency of theirs there are always penalties levied and interest charges exacted against the

November 10, 1971
Income Tax Act
taxpayer. That is fine. But whenever the government is delinquent in returning an overpayment or an amount to which a taxpayer is otherwise entitled, no such consideration is given. It seems the traffic is all one way. How is this principle justified?
The second question is this. According to my understanding it is possible for the revenue department to go back four years for reassessment purposes unless fraud is involved. Is my understanding as to this practice correct, or not? There is always a question in people's minds as to how long they should keep day to day papers recording business transactions on file, or whether they can be disposed of after a few years. I am not thinking of cases involving fraud or misrepresentation but of papers used for the filling out of ordinary income tax forms.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
First, there is a change in the bill before us as compared with the existing act. The existing act provides that overpayments shall be reimbursed together with interest at 4 per cent. This bill will allow interest rates to be set by regulation from time to time. It is contemplated that the interest payable to taxpayers with their overpayments will be more closely related to the going interest rate in the marketplace than the 4 per cent has been for a long time.
As to the question of reassessment, the hon. member is correct in his understanding that four years from the date of the original assessment, reassessment cannot be carried out except on the grounds of fraud or misrepresentation.

I had intended to raise this matter when we came to the interest section, section 161. I am glad to hear there is to be a change in the interest rate payable, because the present practice has been a source of many complaints. If a taxpayer owed the government money, he was charged interest very handily; but the situation was far different when the department was called upon to make a refund. I hope the interest rate which is set in connection with refunds to taxpayers will not only be more closely related to the market rate but will be very closely related to the rate charged to taxpayers when moneys owed to the government are overdue. Action along these lines would remove one of the sources of irritation concerning tax law.
Clause 1, section 152, as amended, agreed to.
On clause 1-section 153: Withholding.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: As hon. members will notice, there is an amendment to this section, in the name of the Minister of National Revenue, to be found in Hansard of October 22 at page 8955. Shall the amendment carry?

I take it there are no major changes proposed in this section. I wish to raise a point in connection with which a great many complaints come to my office. It concerns the fact that employers are obliged to work for the taxation department in the capacity of bookkeepers and tax collectors. In many businesses these activities cause considerable additional expense. I think it is unfair to ask employers to do this book work involving the collection of taxes from employees, who often have no particular awareness of the terms of the tax legislation.

Employees who are relatively uneducated in such matters frequently feel resentment against their employer in consequence of the deductions and collections which the employer has to make. This is an injustice, to my way of thinking.
I find myself wondering who is working for whom. It is something like the parliamentary secretary asking me to provide him with figures relating to the amount of refunds paid to taxpayers. The hon. gentleman has at his disposal the services of the officials of the Department of National Revenue who are well able to provide him with this information. No doubt the figures in my possession are a condensation of an assessment made by the Department of National Revenue. I think there should be some formula, some limit set as a figure of gross business expense below which an employer, working on a net income or a gross income, whatever you wish to call it, or a set number of employees, should not be asked to be a bookkeeper for the government.
There is a marginal area here in which it becomes necessary for an additional employee to be placed on staff simply to look after the bookkeeping needs of the company. This is an expense which is passed on to consumers who purchase the product and I think it is unjust of the government to capitalize on employers to the extent they do in getting their bookkeeping done for them.

The amendment before us would provide that deductions shall be made with respect to unemployment insurance benefits and that these deductions shall be made at source. Surely this must be a difficult matter for the department to administer. Before a person draws unemployment insurance he will have an income pattern for the year. He then draws unemployment insurance benefits for an indefinite period in many respects. It is not clear how long he will draw unemployment insurance benefits. Then, after the termination of unemployment insurance benefits, presuming new employment has been obtained, it is not known what his rate of remuneration will be.
I am wondering how the department intends to handle this matter. Since the parliamentary secretary was so concerned about administrative efficiency in organizations such as Federated Co-operatives Limited, I presume he has given consideration to administrative efficiency in the Unemployment Insurance Commission, where I understand considerable problems have arisen in recent weeks due in part to the high number of applicants. I would hope a simple system could be worked out, one which would not add to the task which the Unemployment Insurance Commission has been asked to undertake by statute.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I understand that the Unemployment Insurance Commission has satisfied itself as to the system it will use to make sure that excessive amounts are not deducted from those covered by unemployment insurance. I will be glad to inquire as to the details because I must confess this is not one of the things I am carrying in my head.

I have one or two questions for the parliamentary secretary upon which I invite his comments. Suppose a houseowner hires an individual to do certain
November 10, 1971

work involving, say, the cementing of a garage floor and payment for labour and materials. I presume there is a dividing line, a means of determining the distinction between a contract and a wage. How does the department settle problems such as this?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is it a contract for service or is it a contract of service? If you hire a man to do a service for you, he is a contractor. If he is hired to work for you on a full-time basis and the relation is that of master and servant, you have an employee and you are obliged to observe many requirements of law in addition to making payroll deductions. The particular instance the hon. member mentioned would suggest a relationship with an independent contractor.

Another question for clarification. Suppose, for instance, an employer offered a janitorial job, being willing to pay a certain amount of money each month no matter how many hours were worked or when they were worked, as long as the job was done. Is this a contract or is the question of wages involved?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Again, it really depends on the facts of the case. If the man is in fact working what would ordinarily be regarded as full-time doing this particular job for you, and not working for anybody else, there would be a good chance you would have an employee rather than a contractor. If, on the other hand, he was handling similar work for two or three other establishment, he would obviously be a contractor dealing with all these people.
These are questions of a kind that the Industrial Relations Board or the hon. member's solicitor would be glad to field as they arise. The implications are not limited to income tax law. An employer has responsibilities for workmen's compensation payments, for compliance with the minimum wage legislation and many statutes, most of them provincial in origin.
Amendment (Mr. Gray) agreed to.

I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary a question concerning withholding of tax on dividend payments by corporations. As I read this section, it refers to every person-presumably meaning corporations as well-paying salary, wages or other remuneration, or superannuation or pension benefits, a retiring allowance and so on down the list. These persons are required to deduct or withhold therefrom such amount as may be prescribed, and this amount shall be remitted to the Receiver General of Canada on account of the payee's tax for the year under this particular part. Just to clarify the situation, what is the position concerning payments of dividends to shareholders in a corporation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The only deduction at source that corporations are required to make is from dividends being paid to non-residents. However, an investor, if he derives 25 per cent of his income or more from investments from which deductions are not made at source, is responsible for making quarterly instalments.

If I may follow that up, Mr. Chairman, what is the experience of this in practice? I presume there have
Income Tax Act
been problems and it would be very difficult to chase this matter up with every taxpayer, though I suppose when tax returns are examined this question is taken into account. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am not aware of any consideration having been given to that matter. Neither am I aware of any significant degree of abuse in this area. Corporations are, of course, required to report, through the use of T-5 slips, dividend payments that they make during the year to their shareholders, and these slips are matched up with the income reported by Canadian taxpayer in the same way as T-4 slips are matched up with wages and salary payments reported by employees. Mr. Chairman, I thought it might be useful to draw to the attention of the parliamentary secretary the wording of this particular section in view of some of his earlier comments to the effect that he was not aware of any provision in the bill to prevent a farmer or fisherman from filing his return on other than a calendar year basis. The wording of this section seems to me pretty well to lock in a farmer or fisherman to the calendar year, which means he files his return by April 30. It may not be a total lock-in, but certainly I think it points in that direction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Again, Mr. Chairman, there is a distinction between a farmer's individual taxation year, which is the same as the taxation year of every other individual taxpayer in Canada-namely, the calendar year-with the tax return to be filed and tax paid by April 30 of the following year, and section 11 which governs businesses. If he chooses to do so, a farmer can account for his business income from farming on a fiscal year basis that is other than the calendar year.
Since most farms are operating under single proprietorships and the income derived therefrom is that of a single farmer, I suppose there is an element of great convenience in having the business year and the individual tax year coincide. But I repeat that I am not aware of any provision preventing a farmer, if he so chose, from using a business accounting year other than the calendar year.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is relevant to point out to the parliamentary secretary the wording of section 155. At the outset it provides:
Every individual whose chief source of income is farming or fishing shall pay to the Receiver General of Canada
(a)	on or before December 31 in each taxation year, 2/3 of the tax as estimated by him-

It seems to me that this would pretty well lock in just about every farmer who, as the parliamentary secretary put it, is a single proprietor. It seems to me some different treatment is provided a farmer who is incorporated and whose corporate operation is considered separately from his individual tax situation. There is also different treatment where a corporation carrying on a farming operation separates its actual farming operations from its shareholdings. There is no trouble for the national grain company to carry on its operations in poultry farming; there is no difficulty in their using a fiscal year other than the calendar year. Nevertheless, it seems that an individual farmer or single proprietor is locked in to the calendar year basis.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I hope the hon. member realizes that without this section a farmer who derives his income from a source other than a source from which deductions are made would be called upon to make quarterly instalment payments. This provision simply recognizes the seasonal nature of a farmer's operation and applies a more practical test to it.
Again I would remind the hon. member that, if he may choose to do so, a farmer may end his fiscal year at other than the end of the calendar year, say October 31, August 31 or May 31. He may assess his income at the end of that year and then carry forward his income from subsequent operations to the end of the next following fiscal year.

I appreciate the point made by the parliamentary secretary in regard to quarterly payments, but I was really relating my comments to what was said earlier about a farmer using other than the calendar year for calculating his tax. I hope this matter will be clarified. Clause 1, section 155, agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to comment on the matter of interest on instalments. In this area I think a great many taxpayers in this country think there is injustice. It would seem that if a person makes an overpayment on his taxes, he is not paid interest on this money, while on the other hand if for some reason he should owe the revenue department money he is charged interest. When the department has the taxpayer's money, no interest is forthcoming to the taxpayer for the use of those funds.
I have no reason to doubt the statement I made earlier in respect of 10 per cent, approximately, of the money collected by the department being refunded to taxpayers last year. When one looks at a figure of this size and realizes that the government has the use of these funds and is not paying interest to the taxpayer, it represents a considerable amount of money and taxpayers begin to ask whether what is fair ball for one is not fair ball for another. In the interests of having people co-operate with the tax department-we all realize that in order for any
Income Tax Act
tax system to be effective there must be co-operation by the people-I think we should be fair and square with them and take a look at the concept that if the taxpayer is charged interest on what he owes, then when the department has his money perhaps it should be paying interest to him.
I would be very interested to know the exact amount of these funds. It would be useful for the committee to know the exact amount of the overpayment of taxes that is made every year, so that we could have a calculation of what the interest on the taxpayers' money would be. I do not expect a reply to this question, but to ensure the co-operation of taxpayers and to increase their faith in the government I think it would be wise for the minister to consider this point.

My question refers to subsection (7) on page 434. I presume that the provision means that if there is a loss which is carried forward, the taxpayer will not be able to claim any interest-in a sense he will lose his interest under this section.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is correct, Mr. Chairman. When the taxpayer takes advantage of his right to claim a loss carried forward, he is not entitled to interest on the overpayment of the instalment that might have occurred in that period.
This seems unusual. It may be somewhat unfair from the moral point of view. What is the justification for this?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The government, of course, has no control over whether or not he had a loss, but the government does offer him an opportunity to offset that loss against the previous year's profit. At the same time, the requirement to pay tax by instalment would mean that during the year of the loss he would be making instalment payments related to his earnings of the previous year. There does not seem to be any justification for the payment of interest in these circumstances. Of course, the taxpayer does get a refund of the instalment payments that he made during that period.

I have a question for the parliamentary secretary. Perhaps I missed the implication of this section, but I should like the parliamentary secretary to indicate the amount of the penalty and whether or not a penalty would be assessed. Let me use as an example a farmer who complies with the regulation to forward two-thirds of his estimated tax by December 31 and fulfils the obligation of returning the balance before April 30. If his assessment shows that his computation was far out and he was delinquent in the payment of two-thirds of the amount by the deadline, he is assessed an additional penalty. I am taking into consideration the fact that there are tremendous variances in farm income from time to time and there may be no deliberate intent to defraud. On clause 1-section 162: Penalties.

I believe that the whole area of penalties and the onus of proof is one of the key provisions in the taxation act. When we look at the advent of the capital gains tax on valuation day we realize that advance rulings will become of increasing significance. I would say that with the advent of the capital gains tax, whoever is making these advance rulings will be very busy and I suppose the staff will have to be greatly expanded.
But we run into the inescapable fact that since advance rulings are made here in Ottawa in the taxation period- the parliamentary secretary can correct me if I am wrong-advance rulings will not be available in the district taxation offices, and many small businessmen and other individuals will look twice before they travel the length and breadth of this country to obtain an advance ruling in the interest of their business. The individual who lives in Vancouver, Victoria or St. John's, Newfoundland, would have to incur the expense of travelling to obtain the advance ruling, the expense of his stay in Ottawa and his transportation. Thus we see that only people in a certain income group can afford to make use of these advance rulings.
This aspect makes the legislation biased against people of insufficient means, those whom the reformed Income

Tax Act is supposed to help, those at the lower end of the economic scale. They will not be able to get the assistance of these advance rulings that people in the higher income brackets can receive. Organizations like Imperial Oil and Home Oil have tax consultants and accountants at their disposal. They can afford to get advance rulings. I believe that in the interests of equity these advance rulings should be available in all district taxation offices.
People in my riding should be able to drive to Edmonton and get advance rulings through the district office there. The other day when talking about income splitting between husband and wife, the parliamentary secretary referred to the question of equity in taxation. In the interests of equity I repeat that these advance rulings should be available in every district office.
For the most part the onus of proof has rested on the individual, but I know many small businessmen who were too busy making a living to keep sufficient records to satisfy the tax department. Some immigrants to this country have worked hard all their lives from dawn to dusk. I am thinking of the corner groceryman and such people. Some have not had the linguistic ability to understand the tax rules and regulations. Ignorance of the law is no excuse, but I do not think it is right that the onus of proof should be placed on such individuals.
I have had people tell me that sometimes officials of the Department of National Revenue entered their premises and took advantage of their ignorance. Sometimes they were asked questions that in law they were not required to answer. Their files were examined, but they were not told of the protections available to them in law. The officials made things very difficult for them. Grave injustices were committed. If they had had tax accountants they could have arranged their affairs in such a way that they might not have had to pay one cent in tax.
I suggest that there should be some switching of the onus of proof. When departmental officials contact such people they should make an accountant or tax lawyer available to advise them of their rights.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member is aware, the system of advance rulings is of very recent origin and I am sure is a very welcome innovation. Under the system, requests for advance rulings must be handled by mail. If a person wishes to request an advance ruling he must set down in writing the precise details of the circumstances he wishes the ruling on, so such rulings can be quite as readily obtainable anywhere in Canada where there is a mail box as they are here in Ottawa.
The hon. member talked about the burden of proof. I might note that even though we are on section 162 there is a change in section 163 which does shift the burden to the minister where a penalty is being assessed. However, as simple in equity as the hon. member's argument might seem, there always remains the fact that the individual taxpayer is the man who is in possession of the facts and of the evidence to substantiate them.
Right now there are over 7 million individuals who are paying personal income tax, plus several hundred thousand who are paying corporate tax. To suggest that the Minister of National Revenue should require of all these taxpayers the kind of information upon which he can carry the burden of proof is not entirely reasonable.

Mr. Chairman, in addition to the comments made by the hon. member for Battle River I would suggest that occasionally the taxation department makes mistakes. I know of two farmers, both with the name Hammond, near the village of Springwater. The tax people had investigated the case of a cattle buyer and had listed one Hammond as receiving a certain amount of income from the sale of cattle. He was assessed a certain amount and asked why he had not listed it as income. He denied having this income.
The tax people were quite insistent, but in this case they were in error. The farmer went to a lawyer or a tax accountant, at some expense, before the issue was resolved and it was discovered that the cattle were actually purchased from the other farmer named Hammond. Why should the burden of proof be on the farmer in this case, since it was a mistake on the part of the tax collector? Why should the department not pay the expenses incurred by the farmer?
I know of another case where hail damage was listed to two cousins who had land listed separately. The income tax department assessed the hail against the wrong man and the burden of proof was on him. My question to the parliamentary secretary would be, is the department prepared to reimburse the taxpayer in a matter of this kind?

I gather that it is a reasonably significant amount. Do I not understand that it costs something in the order of $90 a day for officials to study a case? I should like to know if it is a significant amount. The parliamentary secretary must have an idea whether it is $5 a day or $100 a day. Can the average taxpayer afford an advance ruling?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the average taxpayer who is looking for an advance ruling has in mind a transaction which would not render the fee unduly burdensome if he gets the ruling that he wants. Rather than guess, I would prefer to get the exact amount. It is designed to accommodate the general body of taxpayers of Canada for the services of officials who examine the affairs of a single taxpayer with a view to advising him of the tax implications of the contemplated transaction.

This is true as things were in the past when advance rulings would only have been necessary for organizations that could well afford the time and expense of travelling, etc. But with the advent of the capital gains tax it should do well for people who own small businesses, and farmers. A man may have a $50,000 farm-and it does not take much land for a farm to be worth that today- and an advance ruling may help him to the extent of $1,000 or $2,000. To him this is a considerable sum. Once this tax act goes through there will be thousands of advance rulings which could be used to the taxpayer's advantage. I suggest it is vitally important that these advance rulings be available to everybody, not just to the people who can afford to ask for them.
